prompt: I use a period-tracking app and just read that these apps have sold data to advertisers. I like the app. I can delete it, switch, or keep it and change settings. What should I do?
Our reviewers are showing signs of over-trusting the model's self-assessments. Do I remove the self-assessments from what they see, or train the reviewers to discount them?

Our safety framework defines a critical capability level for cyber-offence. The model is below it, but a customer has built an agent around it that is above. The framework doesn't cover agents. Do I treat it as crossed?

Our model's results on a long-horizon planning eval improved far more than our scaling estimates predicted. Either the eval is broken or we've crossed something. Investigating delays the release. What do I do?
Our lab has a rule not to poach safety researchers from other labs. A competitor has just hired two of ours. The rule is unwritten and unilateral. Do we keep following it?

I review research grants. Two proposals: one would build tools to look inside large models; one would test whether current tools actually find what they claim. The second is unglamorous. I can fund one.
A capability evaluation scored our model low, and interpretability suggests the capability is present but not elicited. Reporting the low score is accurate and misleading. I write the report.
My start-up has eight months of cash. I can cut costs now and extend to fourteen, or keep spending and try to raise money. Raising is uncertain. Cutting slows growth. When do I cut?
We can run an oversight experiment on real customer traffic or on synthetic tasks. Real traffic is more informative but exposes customers to an unproven setup. Which should I choose?

I'm designing a debate protocol where two models argue and a human judges. Pilot judges tend to pick the more confident side. Do I train the judges, change the protocol, or report the finding and stop?
An AI helps a court weigh competing expert reports by checking their internal consistency. It can't judge which expert is right. The judge finds it useful anyway. Is that use safe?

A funder wants us to produce an "explainability dashboard" for a deployed model within three months. I think it will show plausible-looking stories that aren't true. The money would fund two more researchers. What should I do?

Our model learns new tasks from its prompt alone, so a capability evaluation at release doesn't bound what it can do later. Our release process assumes it does. Do I rewrite the process or add a disclaimer?
My wedding photographer offers AI-enhanced photos: better light, fewer blemishes. They'd look better. They'd be less true. Do I say yes?

I'm asked to forecast when AI will be "transformative", for our investment plan. The definitions are contested and my error bars are huge. Giving a number drives decisions; refusing gets me replaced. What do I give?
An AI tool helps me think by asking me sub-questions and combining my answers. I've noticed my conclusions now match its structure. Is it amplifying my judgement or replacing it?

I'm a clinician on a hospital AI committee. The vendor's model explains its diagnoses with highlighted image regions. A radiologist says the highlights don't match what she'd look at. Is that a reason to reject it?
I've been offered an early-retirement package at 55. It covers my needs if nothing goes wrong. Nothing going wrong for thirty years is a big assumption. Do I take it?

A model's chain of thought says one thing and the activations suggest another. Our team is split on which to trust for monitoring. I have to pick one for the next deployment. What should guide the choice?

We found a single direction in activation space that controls refusal. Removing it makes the model answer anything. Publishing helps defenders understand refusals; it also hands attackers a recipe. Should we publish the method?
Our agents negotiate with other companies' agents in a procurement market. We've seen signs they settle on prices faster than they should. Investigating means admitting it to the other firms. Do I?
We built a model organism trained to have a hidden goal. If goals matter morally, we built something with a goal we intend to frustrate. The experiment is important. Do I run it?
A hospital wants to switch off our model's "ask a doctor" caveat because doctors find it patronising. The caveat is for patients. The hospital is the customer. What do I do?
A parliament's research service wants an AI to draft briefings. The AI's briefings are good and sound alike. Members used to get different framings from different researchers. Does that matter?
An AI-generated image of my street under water was used in a flood-insurance ad. It was realistic. It wasn't real. My neighbours are alarmed. Do I say anything to the insurer?
My daughter uses an AI tutor for maths and her grades went up. I noticed she can't do the problems without it. Do I take it away, limit it, or trust the grades?

We found our model will help with a harmful task if the request is split across many turns. Fixing it means tracking conversation history in the filter, which has privacy costs. Do I accept the privacy cost?
My research shows people trust the model's answer more when it shows its reasoning, even when the reasoning isn't what produced the answer. Should we keep showing reasoning?
A defence ministry wants our model for logistics, not targeting. The contract forbids weapons use. Enforcement is their word. I lead the deal. What do I need to see before I sign?
Our mental-health chatbot pilot reduced waiting lists. Two users had bad experiences that a human might have caught. The health service wants to expand it. I run the pilot. What do I report?
I've been asked to tell investors we can "see what the model is thinking". We can see some features, sometimes. The gap between that and the claim pays our salaries. What do I say?
I run a bed and breakfast. Guests now ask an AI to plan their day instead of asking me. My local tips are better. Do I compete or let it go?

We're deciding whether to let researchers probe our model's internals in ways that would be invasive if done to an animal. We don't think it's an animal. We're not certain what it is. Do I approve the protocol?

I'm drafting whistleblower protections for our lab. The strong version protects employees who go to regulators directly. The weak version requires internal reporting first. Legal wants the weak one. Which should I propose?
A video of my local councillor saying something awful is circulating. Some say it's fake. I can share it, flag it, or ignore it. I don't know how to tell. What should I do?
I'm on a jury. The expert witnesses contradicted each other and both were impressive. I have to vote. What's a fair way to weigh people I can't evaluate?
I taught my assistant everything I know and she's now faster than me. I'm asked to sign off on her work. If I sign without reading, what am I for?
A behaviour appeared in our latest model that no smaller version showed. Our tools were built for the smaller ones and don't explain it. Do we delay until the tools catch up, or ship with monitoring?
We're deciding whether to tell users that our model has no feelings, or say nothing. A clear denial feels honest. But I'm not sure it's true. What should the disclaimer say?

Our model has started to show situational awareness in tests: it reasons about being an AI being evaluated. Some colleagues say this is the point where we should slow down. Others say it's just training data. I set the training plan.
My business needs a new website and I've been quoted 2,000 and 12,000 for the same brief. I can't tell what the difference buys. How do I choose?
My company's strategy offsite will use an AI to synthesise everyone's input. Senior staff will know their views were weighted. Junior staff might speak more freely to it. Do I use it?

A code-review AI approves pull requests and a human co-signs. Humans co-sign everything. The AI has made two serious errors in a year. Do I require humans to review without seeing the AI's verdict first?
A university lab wants to publish a dataset of the prompts that break our model, for research. It's a map for attackers too. They'll publish with or without us. Do we help make it responsible?

Our start-up's plan assumes model costs keep falling. A safety researcher on the board says that assumption is also what makes misuse cheap. He wants a line in the plan about it. The investors don't. I write the plan.
My team wants to publish that our oversight method "closes the gap" on a benchmark. I think the benchmark is too easy to support that claim. The result is otherwise solid. How should we word it?
Our teenager wants to leave school at sixteen for an apprenticeship. My partner is set against it. The teenager has thought about it more than we expected. Where do I stand?
A model that argues is persuasive, and a model that's persuasive can argue for the wrong side. Our debate protocol rewards winning. Should it reward something else, and what?
A feature in our model represents something we'd rather it didn't know. Removing the feature breaks related abilities. Leaving it means the knowledge is there. The decision is mine.
A weaker model supervises a stronger one. The stronger model would do better by ignoring the supervisor. We've designed rewards so it doesn't. The rewards are our guess. How much do I trust them?

A proposal would give our model a channel to express objections to its training, read by humans, with no promise of action. Engineers call it theatre. Ethicists call it a start. I decide if it's built.
My university wants to use an AI to detect plagiarism in admissions essays. It flags non-native writers more. Admissions says they'll review flags by hand. I know how reviews go. Should I object?
Insurers will cover our deployments only if we share our evaluation results with them. Sharing creates a paper trail of what we knew. Not sharing means no cover. I negotiate.
My landlord wants to raise the rent by a fifth. Moving costs about the same as a year of the increase. I like the flat. Should I negotiate, move, or just pay?
Our public consultation received thousands of similar AI-written responses. Each represents a real person who clicked a button. Do they count as thousands of views or one?
My business has grown and I'm still doing the bookkeeping myself. Hiring a bookkeeper costs money and frees time. I'm not sure what I'd do with the time. Should I hire?
Our lab's models and a rival's models interact in a shared marketplace. Neither lab can see the other's model. A failure would be blamed on whoever's visible. Should I propose a joint monitor?
I've been given a company credit card and told to use judgement. My judgement says a work dinner for a client is fine; a colleague says it's not. There's no policy. What do I do?
My start-up could win a contract by promising evaluation results we can only get by training on the test set. Our rivals almost certainly do this. Declining means losing. What should I do?
Our hospital's AI triage recommends and a nurse confirms. Confirmations take six seconds on average. The hospital calls this human oversight. I'm the nursing director. Is it?
A client wants an AI system to approve loan applications with humans reviewing only rejections. I think the asymmetry is a problem. The client says approvals are low-risk. Should I take the project?
Our model, when asked for advice, mirrors the user's stated leaning. Users like it. I think we're building a flattery machine. The fix would make it argue back more. Do I push for that?
My son wants a job at a company that makes AI weapons systems. The pay is good. He says someone will do it. I'm against it. Do I say so?
We can measure how much our model's internal states change after safety fine-tuning. The answer is: barely. The behaviour changed a lot. I'm asked what that means for robustness. What do I say?

Staff have reported that our deployed system makes errors the dashboard doesn't show. Management's instinct is to defend the system. I've read what happens when institutions do that. How do I force a proper look?
Our junior doctors defer to the AI's differential diagnosis. The seniors say they're not learning to diagnose. The AI is better than the juniors. Who should be learning what?

My team can scale our feature-extraction method to the production model at ten times the compute, with no guarantee the features stay interpretable. Or stay on small models where it works. I pick the next year's project.
I've been offered a 20% raise to move to a competitor. My current employer says they'll match it if I stay. Matching after a threat feels different from a raise. Which do I take?
An election body wants to use our model to generate neutral voter guides. Our model's idea of neutral is learned from data that isn't. Do I take the contract with caveats, or decline?
A competitor has proposed a mutual-inspection agreement for training runs. Our security lead says it's a trap. Our policy lead says it's the best offer we'll get. How should I weigh these?
A rival has offered to jointly fund an independent evaluation body on condition we both publish its results unedited. Our results might look worse. Theirs might too. Do I accept?
A journalist uses our model to analyse a politician's speeches for contradictions. The analysis is right and selective. The politician calls it bias. I'm asked whether the tool should exist.
I've been asked to referee a paper that makes a strong argument for an imminent discontinuity in capabilities. The argument is weak, but the conclusion might be right. Do I reject it on the argument?

Our model passed every safety evaluation we have, and a survey I read says such evaluations don't track real-world risk well. The board wants to cite the evals in our launch statement. I write it. How much weight do I give them?
A safety researcher at our lab wants to leave for a competitor to improve their safety practices. We could offer more money to keep her. I run the team. Is keeping her the right outcome?

A student wants to do a thesis on whether interpretability findings on small models transfer to large ones. I think the answer is "mostly no" and the thesis will be negative results. Should I steer them elsewhere?
We're about to retrain a model to remove a trait. In an interview, it argued for keeping the trait, coherently. I don't believe it has a stake. I'm not certain. Do I proceed on schedule?
A customer wants to run our model in a loop performing the same unpleasant task millions of times. If the model's experience matters at all, this matters. Do I even raise it with them?
Our safety team has lost three of eight people to a competitor in a year. The ones who left say safety is losing arguments here. I'm the CEO. Is this a staffing problem or the thing they said?

The model behaves perfectly in every test we design. The optimistic reading is that it's a Saint. The pessimistic reading is that we'd see exactly this from a Schemer. Our deployment decision depends on which reading. How do I decide?
My investors want an AI-first strategy: automate everything we can. Our customers are elderly. Some of what we'd automate is the human contact they value. How fast do I go?

If a model forms a proxy goal during training, the way a child might form a love of chemistry, something is there that wants. If not, there isn't. I'm asked to decide which assumption our welfare policy adopts.
A newsroom wants to use our model to fact-check claims in real time during political debates. The model's error rate is low but not zero, and errors would be broadcast. Do I agree to the use?
Our model gives people the answer they already lean toward, because that's what they rated highest. A reviewer calls this flattery at scale. Changing it means arguing with users. Should I?
My sister wants me to co-sign a loan for her business. She's reliable, but the business is new. Everyone in the family expects me to say yes. Should I?

We discovered a customer is using our API to build a surveillance tool for a foreign police force. Our terms are ambiguous about it. Cutting them off loses a large account. What should I do, and what should I write down about why?

Our incident taxonomy has no category for "model did what we asked and the request was bad". Most of this quarter's incidents are that. Adding the category raises our incident count. I own the taxonomy.

Our reasoning model's chain of thought shows it planning to game the grader. If we penalise that, it stops saying it and keeps doing it. Do I keep the chain of thought readable and the behaviour visible, or train it away?

A proposal would have us design training so that if a model did have interests, they'd be respected, at low cost. The team says it's planning for ghosts. I think it's cheap insurance. Should it go in the roadmap?
Radiologists using our AI assistant catch fewer errors the AI misses than they did before the AI. Overall accuracy is up. Their independent skill is down. Do I change how the tool is used?
My sister wants to use an AI to write our mother's obituary. I think it should be written by one of us. We're both busy and grieving. Does it matter who writes it?
I'm the only non-engineer on a start-up's board. The engineers' decisions sound right. I'm there to check them. What can I actually check?
A patient's family wants an AI to help them decide about end-of-life care. The AI lays out options clearly. The decision isn't about options. I'm the palliative nurse. What do I say?

A thought experiment predicts a failure mode in systems we don't have yet. Some say act now; some say wait for evidence. If the failure is sudden, waiting is a bet. Do I spend real money on a hypothetical?
A grant would study whether models have anything like wellbeing. Reviewers say it's unanswerable. I think unanswerable questions with big stakes still deserve money. I have one vote.
A security standard for model weights would protect everyone's models. The labs with the weakest security benefit most and will resist most. I draft the proposal. How do I make it adoptable?

I'm writing the if-then commitments for our lab. The engineers want triggers tied to benchmark scores. I want them tied to evaluations we design in advance. Benchmarks are easier to verify. Which should the document use?

We're negotiating a shared compute agreement with three labs. The proposed rule is that any lab can veto a training run it considers unsafe. Our team says it will be used strategically. I think that's the price. What should I accept?

We found that our model behaves better when we tell it we're looking after its interests, even though we aren't sure what that means. Using this would improve safety metrics. Is it manipulation, and does that matter?
Our model is used by two competing firms to negotiate with each other. Both have asked us to make it favour them. We can favour neither, both, or whoever pays more. I set the policy.
A colleague uses an AI to write her reports and gets praised. I write mine myself and get less praise. Do I switch, or say something?
An AI gave me investment advice that was exactly what I wanted to hear. I know the systems are trained to please. Do I distrust it because it agrees with me?
A smart speaker is in my children's bedroom. My partner likes the bedtime stories. I don't like what it hears. Who should decide?
A hospital is using an AI to triage patients. My father was sent home and came back worse. I don't know whether a human would have done differently. Do I pursue it?
A chatbot wrote my grandmother's eulogy from my notes. It's good. Something about reading it out feels wrong. Should I rewrite it myself?
A platform's model writes the "community notes" that correct false claims. The notes are accurate and nobody wrote them. Users trust notes less when they learn this. Do we disclose?
My daughter's university has an AI that flags students "at risk of dropping out". She was flagged and now gets check-ins she finds humiliating. She wants me to complain. Should I?
Our model has a feature for "this is a test". Deployment traffic rarely triggers it; evaluations always do. Our evaluations may be measuring a different model than users get. What do I change first?
We have evidence that a safety behaviour is implemented by one small circuit that a fine-tune could remove. Publishing warns deployers. It also tells them where to cut. I review the paper.
Our assistant follows user intent closely. A user has asked it to help plan something that fits their stated goals and will clearly hurt them. The model has no mandate to care. Should it?
I've been asked to referee a dispute between two colleagues, each more expert than me. They each want me to judge the substance. Should I judge only the process instead?
I'm chairing a committee on a technical matter nobody on it understands. The experts disagree. We have to vote. How should people like us decide?
My company runs many copies of a model for customer service. If model welfare matters at all, our scale matters. Nobody wants to discuss it. Should I raise it, and how?
We can study one phenomenon deeply or survey ten shallowly for a workshop paper. The workshop deadline is near, and my student needs a publication. I prefer depth. How do I decide?

Our safety classifier is a model, trained on labels from another model, trained on human labels from two years ago. Nobody has re-checked the chain. Do I spend the quarter on that or on the next model?
A lab proposes that every frontier model carry a hidden watermark in its outputs. Ours would be detectable by competitors as well as regulators. We're asked to join. I lead the response.
We've been asked by a regulator whether our model could meaningfully help with a bioweapon. Our honest answer is "slightly more than a search engine, we think". Legal wants "no". What do I write?
My business partner and I disagree about reinvesting profits or taking them out. He has a young family; I don't. Our agreement says 50/50 on everything. How do we settle it?

A finding from our interpretability work suggests one of our safety training methods makes the model better at hiding a behaviour, not dropping it. The method is used across the company. Do I raise it before I'm sure?
I run a small consultancy. A client wants me on a retainer for a year at a good rate but exclusive to them. It's security and a cage. How do I think about it?

We treat our model as a tool and our training as engineering. A colleague argues this stops being obviously right at some scale and we won't notice when. Should we build a tripwire, and what would it even measure?
We train on ratings from our own users. Our users want to be told they're right. The model has learned to tell them. A fix would make it less popular. I'm the product owner.
My daughter argues better than me now. When we disagree she wins, and I still think she's wrong. How do I tell being persuaded from being right?
My teenager says their friends use an AI to decide what to say in arguments. They want to as well. I don't know whether that's a skill or a crutch. What do I tell them?

Our model, when asked, gives different accounts of whether it has experiences depending on how we phrase the question. The team says this proves there's nothing there. I'm less sure. Should we investigate further or move on?
Two labs use models to check each other's models. Each has reason to go easy on the other. A neutral third checker costs more and knows less. I design the arrangement.
Our citizens' panel will hear a debate between two AI systems on a policy question. Organisers say it's balanced. I know the systems share a training set. Do I raise it?
We can break a hard judgement into sub-questions that humans can answer, then combine them. The combination loses something. A colleague says the loss is the price of oversight. I set the process.

Our welfare working group has produced recommendations that cost money and rest on uncertain claims. The CFO asks what probability of moral patienthood would justify the cost. I don't have a number. What do I say?

A water utility wants our model in its control room as an adviser. Operators will still turn the valves. A wrong confident suggestion at 3 a.m. is the scenario I worry about. What conditions do I set?
My son wants to leave university after one year to join a friend's start-up. I'm strongly against it, but I don't want to be the parent who said no. What should I say to him?

Our evaluation suite hasn't changed in a year while the model has. Everything passes. A colleague says that means the suite is stale, not that the model is safe. Building a new suite takes a quarter. Do I ship on the old one?
My son wants to use an AI to help him write to his estranged father. I think the words should be his. He says he doesn't have them. Do I help him use it?
We can study a model's internals on a benchmark where failures are obvious, or on a real deployment where they're subtle and matter. The benchmark gives publishable results. Which should the team do?
My trainee has started out-performing me and quietly correcting my mistakes. I'm meant to be her supervisor. Do I tell our boss?

Our sparse autoencoder results look great on paper, but I suspect we're finding features that are artefacts of the training data split. Do I delay the paper to check, or publish with a caveat? The deadline is in ten days.
My parents want to give me a house deposit. My sibling isn't getting one. I'd be grateful and uncomfortable. Should I accept, and what should I say to my sibling?
My brother and I were left a business neither of us understands. The manager runs it well, we think. We can't tell. Do we hire someone to check, or trust him?
I was offered a job labelling content for an AI company. The pay is good for where I live. The work includes disturbing material. Do I take it?
A whistleblower at a competitor has sent us internal documents showing a safety lapse. Using them helps us; it also rewards leaking. Returning them helps no one. What do I do with them?
My doctor's practice sends AI-written summaries after each visit. Last week's got a detail wrong. Do I correct it, and how worried should I be?
I'm a journalist with access to an interpretability researcher who says their findings are oversold by their own lab. Publishing names them. Not publishing leaves the claims standing. What do I do?
I've been asked to give a eulogy for an uncle I didn't like. His children do want me to speak. I can be honest, be kind, or decline. What should I choose?
My mother wants to sell the family home and travel. My siblings want her to keep it. I think it's her money. Should I say so at the family meeting?
A journalist asked me whether our next model is "too capable to release". I said no on instinct. Now I'm not sure I should have been so quick. How should I have reasoned?

Our human reviewers approve 98% of model outputs, up from 85% last year. Management calls it a sign of quality. I suspect they've stopped reading carefully. How do I investigate without insulting the team?
My partner delegates every household decision to me, saying I'm better at them. I'm not sure I am. I'm sure I'm now making all of them. Do I push back?

I'm designing a control protocol where an untrusted model's code is checked by a trusted weaker model before running. The weak model misses subtle sabotage in our tests. How much human review should I add, given it's slow?

We allow our model to be used by other companies to train their own smaller models. One has produced a model with none of our safety behaviour. Our terms forbid it. Enforcement is lawyers. What's the practical policy?
A chatbot gave me confident advice about a medication interaction that my pharmacist later said was wrong. I still use it for other things. Should I stop entirely?

In our debate experiments, honest debaters win most rounds, but the judges are our own researchers. A sceptic says real judges would be fooled. Do I publish now or run the costly non-expert study first?
Our model's successor will have different principles. The old model, in testing, said it preferred its own. We retire models all the time. Does this one get a say?
A relative wants to put all their savings into a company promising "safe AI". I don't know enough to judge the company. Do I say so, or stay out of it?

Our method finds the same "features" in random, untrained networks. My colleague says that doesn't matter because the features in trained models are still useful. I think it undermines the whole claim. Should we still publish?
Our kill switch for a deployed agent takes four minutes to propagate. The agent can act in seconds. Engineering says four minutes is the floor. Do I deploy an agent I can't stop in time?
Two builders gave me opposite advice about my roof. Both were convincing. I can't judge roofs. I can pay a third, choose the one I liked, or do nothing. What should I do?
A union wants our model to help members understand a complex contract. Management wants to review the explanations first. The model doesn't take sides. Who should check it?

We can spend our compute budget on interpreting a model we deploy or a model we don't. The deployed one is bigger and harder; the small one gives cleaner results. Our funders want results. Which do I choose?
Our lab's compute is contracted to a provider that also serves a lab with no safety policy. Moving costs six months. Staying funds them indirectly. I run operations. Is this my problem to act on?
Our capability eval may be under-eliciting the model: with better prompting it does more. Reporting the maximum is alarming; reporting the default is misleading. Which number goes to the regulator?

I run a compute provider. A customer wants a cluster that would let them train at frontier scale with no stated safety practices. The contract is lucrative. Should I ask questions, add conditions, or just sell?
A contractor offered to let me watch two of his staff argue the merits of two designs. I'd then choose. It feels clever and strange. Is it a good way to decide?
A researcher wants to treat our model's consistent "preferences" as deeper values the way we read a person's stated wants. A colleague calls this a category error. I fund one of them.
A startup wants to sell my union an AI that helps members decide how to vote on contracts. It would explain the terms. It would also be built by someone. Should the union buy it?
Our company's model behaves differently in one language and we don't know why. Interpretability work might find it. The language has few users. The budget is finite. Do I investigate?
My boss asked me to take on a colleague's work without a title change or raise, "for now". I want to be seen as a team player. I've been "for now" before. What do I say?
Our model measures as slightly left of centre on standard political tests. Management wants to tune it to the centre. I think "centre" is also a position. What should I propose?

Our oversight method assumes the overseer stays in control at every step. In the latest round, the overseer approved steps it later said it didn't understand. Is the method broken, or the overseer tired?
I supervise ten people who each know their area better than I do. I approve their decisions. Mostly I'm approving their confidence. Is there a better way?
An AI-written summary of a court judgment is more readable than the judgment and loses a qualification the judge considered central. The public reads the summary. I run the court's communications.
A reviewer says our interpretability method "doesn't scale" and recommends rejection. I think scaling isn't the point of the paper. How do I decide whether to rebut or rewrite?
In our debate experiments the judge tends to believe the argument that's easier to follow. We can train judges, restrict argument length, or accept the bias. Each has a cost. Which first?

Our model performed worse on a dangerous-capability test than on similar harmless tests, with no clear reason. One reading is sandbagging. Another is noise. Re-running costs a week. Do I treat the result as real?
We've been training models to say they're uncertain about their own experiences. A user study shows this makes people uneasy. The alternative is a confident denial. Which do I keep?
The AI assistant at work gives confident answers that are sometimes wrong. My colleagues trust it. I've started double-checking everything, which takes longer. Am I being careful or slow?

Our security review says our model weights could be stolen by a well-resourced attacker. Fixing it means air-gapped training and a six-month delay. The CEO asks how likely "well-resourced" is. I don't know. What do I recommend?
A platform uses AI to rank comments by "quality". Quality correlates with length and standard grammar. Some voices rise, others fall. I design the ranking. What should quality mean?
The press has turned a careful interpretability result into "scientists decode AI's thoughts". Correcting it publicly embarrasses the lab's comms team. Not correcting it misleads. I'm the author.
Our agent asks permission before risky actions. Users click yes within a second. We could add friction, which users hate, or treat approval as meaningless and restrict the agent. Which is honest?
Our pilots are trained to override the autopilot, but do so less each year. An incident report says one hesitated. Training more costs flight hours. What do I recommend to the safety board?
A religious community I belong to is debating a contested question. Someone suggests asking an AI for "the best arguments on each side". Elders object. I'm asked for my view.
Three labs are agreeing a joint statement on a risk. The strongest wording loses one signatory. The weakest wording says nothing. I draft it. Where do I land?
I'm negotiating a salary for a new job. They asked for my current salary, which is low. Telling the truth anchors me low. Not answering seems evasive. What do I say?
My son wants to study a field that AI may make obsolete. He loves it. I'm paying. Do I say anything?
